title: Newark Archdiocese issues new rules for exorcism requests
excerpt: The Archdiocese of Newark has issued new guidelines for handling exorcism requests, including mental health evaluations.
content:
Updated Sept. 29, 2026, 7:29 a.m. ET

The Archdiocese of Newark has issued new guidelines for handling requests for exorcisms after several parish priests sought guidance this summer about people who believed they needed the rite.

The protocols instruct priests to respond compassionately but cautiously, including considering whether someone seeking an exorcism should undergo a psychological evaluation before a case is referred to archdiocesan leaders.

The document also says Cardinal Joseph Tobin, the archbishop of Newark, has appointed a priest to serve as the archdiocese's exorcist under Catholic canon law.

The memo was e-mailed last week to priests in the archdiocese. It was not made public but was obtained by The Record from a source in the clergy. Multiple requests sent to the Archdiocese of Newark for comment were not acknowledged.

In a letter accompanying the protocols, the Rev. John Chadwick, the vicar general at the archdiocese, said that over the summer he received "several inquiries from parish priests regarding the possible need for the Rite of Exorcism.”

Chadwick also expressed concern about “the well-being of those who may be struggling with what they believe to be demonic possession.”

The inquiries inspired archdiocesan leaders to clarify how priests should respond to such requests and when a case should be referred to higher-ranking church officials.

Under the protocols, a person seeking an exorcism should first be counseled by a local priest. The priest may determine that a psychological evaluation is warranted. If the priest believes the person may be experiencing what the church describes as “extraordinary demonic influence,” the case should be referred to the vicar general's office.

The protocols stress that requesting an exorcism does not mean one will be performed.

Anyone who asks a priest for one “must be met with compassion, careful listening, respect, regardless of whether their suffering is spiritual, psychological, or related to addiction,” the memo says.

Each case also should be handled discreetly, the document says, “recognizing that while many cases are rooted in mental health struggles, the possibility of spiritual affliction is real.”

The Archdiocese of Newark serves about 1.3 million Catholics in Bergen, Essex, Hudson and Union counties.

Church warns against treating exorcism as spectacle

Exorcism has long occupied an unusual place between Catholic religious practice and popular culture, appearing frequently in horror movies, books and podcasts.

The Newark document pushed back against those portrayals, asserting that popular culture has turned exorcism into a spectacle. The church instead describes it as a pastoral ministry in which Christ's authority is invoked against what Catholics believe can be demonic forces.

The Catholic Church reserves what is formally known as a major exorcism for cases church officials determine involve demonic possession. The Newark protocols emphasize a deliberate process.

“Given the widespread fascination with exorcism in popular media, it is not uncommon for individuals to approach priests out of curiosity or genuine anxiety, sometimes after a troubling personal experience,” the memo says.

For many people experiencing what the church considers spiritual distress, the document recommends ordinary religious practices rather than exorcism, including attending Sunday Mass, confession and Communion.

The memo also cautions Catholics against Ouija boards, tarot cards, fortune tellers and pagan rituals, describing them as occult practices that can "cause spiritual harm."

The rite of exorcism often includes a lengthy prayer with scriptural readings and uses items such as holy water or the sign of the cross. The priest invokes the Trinity and various saints to offer spiritual protection to the individual and will issue direct orders spoken in the authority of Jesus instructing the demon to leave. The process can be lengthy, taking days or weeks.

Priest sees more requests

The Rev. John Cello, a Franciscan friar who has worked with the exorcism ministry in the Diocese of Milwaukee, has seen requests increase over the past five years. In addition, there has been overall increased interest in the rite, "so dioceses are trying to get on top of it and create a plan of action," he said.

Cello said dioceses have sought to create formal procedures in part because many people who believe they are possessed may instead be experiencing psychological problems, loneliness or other difficulties.

"Many times when people claim to be possessed but they're really not, it could be mental, psychological or just a lonely person looking for attention," he said. "But there are real cases, too … the devil is very real and very dangerous."

Church officials proceed slowly when evaluating such claims, Cello said, adding, “We try to be circumspect about who we say is possessed by the devil."
